title: The one who fell short
hookLine: Arjuna asks the question under every new habit: what if I start, and fail?
carry: no good effort is lost, even across lifetimes

lines: WHAT IF I START, AND FAIL?
A CLOUD, TORN OFF AND GONE?
A WEEK TO LIVE UP TO.
cards: What about the person who starts with real faith, and can't keep it up? The mind wanders off, and they never get there. Do they lose both worlds?
Are they like a small cloud, torn off from the big one, that just thins out and disappears? That's Arjuna's question, the one anyone asks on day nine of a new habit.

Six days, six big asks: the same self in every body; the peace that doesn't end; lift the self by the self; a clean place, a firm seat; the lamp out of the wind; the restless mind. That's a lot to live up to.

teach.b: A painful picture: you left the ordinary life, didn't reach the spiritual one, and now you're neither. Krishna's answer is gentle. Verse forty: there is no destruction for them, Arjuna, neither here nor in the next world.

teach.h: NO ONE WHO DOES GOOD IS LOST.
teach.b: No one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end. The word he uses there, tata, is tender, the way an elder speaks to a child. Then he tells what happens.
The one who fell short reaches the worlds of the good, and stays long. Then they're born again into a good and prosperous home, or, rarer, into a family of wise yogis.

teach.h: THEY PICK UP WHERE THEY LEFT OFF.
teach.b: There, verse forty-three says, they get back the understanding they had before, and they strive again, harder.
Verse forty-four: they're carried forward by their earlier practice, even without meaning to be.

This is the Hindu teaching of karma and rebirth at its gentlest: what you practice leaves a mark on you, and the mark travels with you. Every sit, every returned thought, every day of practice counts, and it carries.
So the broken streak doesn't erase the days you kept. Through many lifetimes of effort, the yogi comes to the goal.
The chapter ends by lifting the yogi above ascetics, scholars and ritual-doers, and saying that of all yogis, the one who turns to Krishna with faith, the inner self absorbed in him, is the closest.

how: Gita 6.40 is often quoted by Hindu teachers to encourage people who have lapsed in practice; some commentators divide the Gita into three sets of six chapters, and chapter six closes the first.

o: a sacred vow made before a teacher
a word for someone who has failed
my dear, said by an elder to a child

games.q: what's inside the chapter — tap the pairs.
p: a tender word, like to a child
no one who does good comes to ruin

s: the one who fails at yoga loses both worlds
verse 40: there's no destruction for them, here or hereafter.
the Gita says they pick up the understanding they had before
verse 43: they regain it and strive again, harder.
only practice that reaches the goal counts
verse 44: earlier practice carries them forward, even without their meaning it to.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you imagine someone who starts with faith, but their mind wanders and they never arrive. what does Krishna say happens to them?
o: they're lost, like a torn cloud.
nothing is lost; they pick up where they left off.
games.why: nothing is lost. they reach good worlds, are reborn in a good home, regain their earlier understanding, and strive again.

practice: Look back over this week, or this whole path so far, to a day you skipped or a sit that was all wandering, and instead of counting it against yourself, picture it the way verse forty-four does: as momentum.
Every minute you did sit is still moving you. Breathe in and feel it carrying you; breathe out and let the missed days go.

wordCard.voice: Tata. My dear: the tender word Krishna uses for Arjuna. Gita six, forty: the one who strives and doesn't arrive isn't lost; earlier practice carries them forward.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tata, a tender address, 'my dear', used by an elder to a child; Krishna uses it in 6.40.

carryVoice: Your line: no good effort is lost, even across lifetimes. What you practiced is still moving you. That's chapter six, finished.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.37–6.39 (Arjuna's question; the torn cloud)
